sentences.text: Somewhere in your messages there is probably a pitch like this.
A friend you have not heard from in years has started a business, and she would love to have you on her team: you earn from what you sell, and from everyone you bring in after you.

sentences.text: The recruiters have a word for that second part: one trainer, Frazer Brookes, promises to show you how to "finally create the leverage that you need inside of your network marketing business".

sentences.text: So where does the money go, and why does leverage that sounds so good on paper show up in almost nobody's bank account?
This video is about one question: how much money do people in multi-level marketing actually make?
To answer it we have the companies' own numbers first: 70 income disclosure statements, read closely by Federal Trade Commission staff.

sentences.text: Then a nationally representative survey of 601 participants by AARP.

sentences.text: And an analysis of 30 companies by Jon Taylor, an independent analyst who argues against the industry.

sentences.text: Two confident stories, so let us see which one the numbers tell.
Start with the companies, because some of them publish an income disclosure statement, and FTC staff collected 70 of them, from household names to small firms.

sentences.text: Once FTC staff worked through the fine print, the statements with enough data to tell showed most participants received $1,000 or less in a year: under $84 a month.

assertions.text: For the disclosures with enough data for FTC staff to calculate it, most participants had $1,000 or less in reported income for the year, which is less than $84 per month.
qualifications: s17 to s21 say the figures exclude non-earners in most statements and are before expenses in all of them.

sentences.text: In at least 17 of the 70 companies, most participants made nothing at all.

sentences.text: And that is the generous reading, because of three things buried in the fine print.
First, who gets counted: of the 70 statements, 29 leave out participants who earned no commission, and another 24 leave out anyone the company has labelled inactive.

assertions.text: Of the 70 disclosures, 29 exclude from their income distribution participants who earned no commissions, and another 24 exclude participants the MLM deems inactive.

sentences.text: What happens to an average when you remove the zeros before you take it?
Second, what gets counted: not one of the 70 statements reports income with expenses taken out in full, and 20 of them never say whether expenses were taken out at all.

assertions.text: None of the 70 income disclosure statements provides income figures that take expenses into account in full, and 20 of them have no express statement about whether their figures account for expenses.

sentences.text: So the dollar figures are what the company paid out, before most or all of whatever the participant spent to take part.

assertions.text: The disclosed income figures are payments from the MLM and do not account for the expenses participants incurred.

sentences.text: Third, how it is presented: 44 of the 70 break the numbers out only by rank, and in those tables, nearly without exception, the vast majority of participants sit in the two or three lowest ranks.
